new.n: Marion Ogle's hidden gold, farm near Medora
new.pl: GNIS Medora; 'the farm near Medora', direction not given
new.st: Marion Ogle, an eccentric and wealthy farmer, died in 1907 after a runaway accident without regaining consciousness. A few days before, he had brought $10,000 he had hidden about the farm to an Indianola bank; his fortune was put at $50,000 to $80,000 and the popular belief was that more gold was still hidden on the farm, which relatives searched. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself.
new.t: Find Ogle on a 1900s Warren County plat near Medora. One paper so far, so C. Access: private: permission.
src: Twice-a-Week Plain Dealer (Cresco) 2 Aug 1907 p3 (LoC Chronicling America)

new.n: John Meade's gold in baking-powder cans, old barn 9 mi east of Iowa City
new.pl: 'a wealthy farmer nine miles east of town' (Iowa City); pin 9 mi due east, direction approximate
new.st: In August 1911 T. T. Meade found more than $3,000 in $10 and $20 gold pieces packed in old baking-powder cans while tearing down an old barn built by his father John Meade, who had died four years before; the coin dates suggested it was buried about fifteen years earlier. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself.
new.t: Found; a farmer who used cans may have used more than one spot. Find Meade on a 1900s Johnson County plat. Access: private: permission.
src: Oskaloosa Herald 10 Aug 1911 p1 (Iowa City special, LoC Chronicling America)

new.n: Erick Davidson's gold in an old shed, Branstad homestead a mile east of Leland
new.pl: 'the old E. F. Branstad homestead, a mile east of Leland'; pin 1 mi E of GNIS Leland
new.st: Children playing in an old shed on the E. F. Branstad homestead a mile east of Leland found a box of gold; a further search found a second box, $1,024 in gold in all, packed long before. It was believed to be the hidden savings of Erick Davidson, who had lived with the Branstads before his death. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself.
new.t: Found. A second hiding place turned up when they looked again, so more is possible. Access: private: permission.
src: Decorah Public Opinion 18 Jan 1922 p5 (LoC Chronicling America)

new.st: In May 1916 Ruth Stevens of Grandview, cleaning the cellar of her home, moved a barrel and found a $5 gold piece, then about $300 more in gold. An eccentric recluse who had lived on the place years before was believed to have hidden his savings there. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself.

set.n: Fort Crawford soldiers' buried gold, McGregor Heights and the bluffs at McGregor
set.pl: 1913 McGregor account: gold buried 'on one of the hills, supposedly the Heights hill now used as a summer resort' (GNIS McGregor Heights); legend, no fixed spot
set.st: Several versions of one legend. Soldiers from Fort Crawford crossing to McGregor's landing with $8,000 in gold to pay the Fort Atkinson garrison were killed by Indians after burying it on a hill, said to be the Heights; other tellings have a canoe of gold sunk in the Mississippi, a sack buried near Fort Crawford, or $80,000 buried by four of Col. Zachary Taylor's soldiers near North McGregor. Early settlers hunted the hills, and in 1913 a man with a 'gold magnet' came to McGregor to search. Pin is approximate, not the spot itself.
set.t: Legend with no fixed spot. Effigy Mounds National Monument and Pikes Peak State Park nearby are no-dig; McGregor Heights is residential. Access: private / state and federal land near: look only.
src: Decorah Public Opinion 22 Oct 1913 (one 1913 McGregor story, LoC Chronicling America)
